title: Check daily or yearly?
hook: Would you choose the same portfolio after changing the reporting interval?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Explain how aggregating returns changes how often a loss appears without changing the assets.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Explain how aggregating returns changes how often a loss appears without changing the assets.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A €100 account falls 10%, then rises 20%. What is its total return across both periods? Toy inputs A=[-10, 20]; B=[-5, 10].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[8, 1, 108], [4.500000000000014, 1, 104.50000000000001]]. Labels: Net %, Loss periods, Final €.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The period path includes a loss even though the combined return is positive. Aggregating the same asset’s returns changes the reporting window, not the cash flows that produced the ending balance.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Period 1 %=-5, Period 2 %=10. What is Net %? Answer: 4.5.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Period 1 %=-5, Period 2 %=10. What is Net %?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 4.5. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: People shown investment results less often put more money in stocks (Gneezy & Potters, 1997; Thaler, Tversky, Kahneman & Schwartz, 1997).

sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.
